#4526. Kia just made history at Germany’s most prestigious auto awards

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

#4525. Spider-bear? Black cub wins the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

Published Nov 16, 2026 12:15 PM EST

They may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest showed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

#4523. Nuclear submarine returns from record-breaking 217 days underwater

Published Nov 16, 2026 1:05 PM EST

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First launched in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

Vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

Deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

Key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”

The Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

#4520. Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

Three-point seatbelts and a soft-start feature help keep rides secure and smooth. It’s recommended for ages three and up and can carry up to 132 pounds.

For little speed demons with big supercar dreams, this officially licensed Lamborghini STO ride-on delivers serious wow factor. The sleek design mirrors the real exotic sports car, while a powerful 24-volt battery, drift mode, and speeds up to 6 mph make every driveway feel like a racetrack. Parents will appreciate the included remote control and safety features, while kids will love the lights, sounds, and realistic driving experience. Recommended for ages three to eight.

Posh little drivers can cruise in style with this Bentley, available in red, black, green, or white. Working LED headlights, scissor doors, realistic engine sounds, and a high/low speed switch give it plenty of big-car flair. Parents can steer with the remote, too, in case the young racer needs a little help staying on course.

It reaches about 3 mph and offers up to an hour of playtime, depending on speed and terrain. It’s recommended for ages three to six and supports up to 66 pounds.

Little adventure seekers will get a kick out of this replica Jeep, with its LED headlights, lockable doors, grid windshield, and off-road tires. It includes a parent remote, spring suspension, and a safe and manageable max speed of just 2.8 mph. It comes in five colors besides light or dark pink: black, blue, green, red, and white.

While this ride-on Jeep replica claims to be for kids aged three to six, reviewers say that because of the roll bar, it’s actually ideal for younger, smaller kids who can easily slide into the seat. Keep an eye on that weight limit.

This officially licensed G63 brings plenty of grown-up detail to the pint-size package, from exhaust pipes and body decals to doors that open and lock from the outside. A seatbelt and soft-start feature help keep little drivers secure and ease them into motion, while spring suspension smooths out the bumps.

We also like the removable side window: Take it off as your child gets bigger, and the ride-on can keep cruising for longer.

The GoKart Pro 2 adjusts to fit drivers from four foot two to six foot two, with enough battery range to cover up to 15.5 miles. My kids and I had a blast testing it: They eased in with Eco mode’s 5-mph limit, while I switched to Race mode to explore what it could really do around the neighborhood. Four riding modes—Eco, Sport, Race, and Manual—give beginners room to build confidence and experienced drivers more freedom to play.

It’s a serious investment, but the adjustable fit, long range, and genuinely thrilling ride make a strong case for the price.

This officially licensed Silverado Trail Boss gives little drivers a pickup of their own, complete with LED lights, startup sounds, and doors that open. Forward and reverse gears make driveway maneuvers part of the fun, while Bluetooth lets kids bring along a soundtrack. It’s designed for ages 37 to 72 months and holds up to 66 pounds.

This pint-size Range Rover Sport has room for two little adventurers and plenty of big-SUV flair. Working LED headlights, hidden hood storage, and adjustable harnesses add fun and practicality, while a parent remote lets grown-ups lend a hand at the wheel.

It’s also available in blue, pink, red, or white, the 24-volt battery offers up to two hours of playtime, and it’s rated for kids ages three to eight, with a 132-pound weight limit.

Give your little driver a taste of supercar life with this officially licensed Lamborghini Urus ride-on. Inspired by the luxury SUV’s sleek styling, it features working LED lights, opening doors, spring suspension, realistic engine sounds, and built-in music for an immersive driving experience. Kids can take the wheel themselves or let parents guide the fun with the included remote control.

Available in four eye-catching colors, it’s a stylish choice for young car enthusiasts who want to cruise in Lamborghini-inspired fashion.

For kids with dirt dreams, this little red UTV is ready to turn the backyard into a weekend expedition. Its 12-volt battery and dual motors power forward and reverse, while openable doors, LED headlights, a horn, and built-in music add plenty of trucklike fun.

A safety belt, a gentle-start feature, and shock-absorbing tires help keep rides comfortable. It’s designed for kids ages three and up and supports up to 66 pounds.

Ever see a kid’s toy and wish you’d had one when you were that age? That’s the way this mini John Deere has us feeling. It’s got two speeds—2.25 and 4.5 mph—plus reverse. (High speed can be disabled for beginners.) It operates via an accelerator pedal and has farmlike tractor wheels for traction on grass, dirt, gravel, or pavement. It also has a cool stake-side trailer and (get this!) a working FM radio. All that’s supercool, but we love the fact that it recharges in just two hours (claimed).

Featuring sirens, speakers, and flashing police lights, this Fire Chief SUV gives children the most realistic experience of driving a fire truck. It’s designed for kids aged three to six years, with a maximum weight capacity of 67 pounds.

Little land movers will feel right at home in this ride-on dump truck. It’s the ultimate fun machine. With two 35-watt motors, it features two speeds when manually controlled by the child using the foot pedal and three speeds (top speed 3 mph) with the parent remote control. It also has a built-in Bluetooth speaker and a working dump bed.

With automatic lifting and an extra shovel, kids can pitch in with the yardwork by carrying leaf piles and debris.

Let’s be clear: This is not a toy for young kids. Older kids, though, will love these little electric motorcycles. Available in MX and SX packages, with 350-, 500-, or 650-watt motors, they come in blue, yellow, or green. The 350-watt version (ages 13 and up) can hit speeds up to 14 mph for about 30 minutes of ride time; the 650 (16 and up) jacks that to about 17 mph with around 45 minutes of ride time; the 500 (14 and up) falls in the midrange. Pricing is relative. All feature dual suspension and riser handlebars, pneumatic knobby tires, a retractable kickstand, and hand-operated dual disc brakes.

While all are undeniably cute and cool, it’s important to reiterate that these Razor electric bikes are not toys designed for small children. Helmets are mandatory—and professional rider training is a good idea.

If your kid is ready to take to the not-so-open road, here’s what to look for in a kids’ electric car.

While it can be tempting to get a ride-on that your child will grow into and use for years, there are safety risks involved with choosing one that’s too large or powerful for your kid to control easily. Check the manufacturer’s recommendations for age and weight. Some even offer parental remote controls and seatbelts, while others let you remove features like side panels as your child grows.

Electric ride-ons come in multiple styles to match kids’ varying interests. Classic cars and trucks mimic real-life vehicles, offering features like working headlights and sound effects for a realistic experience. ATVs and UTVs are built for rougher terrain with “all-terrain” tires and higher clearances. For kids who love motorcycles, bike-style ride-ons can often include training wheels for added stability.

Most electric ride-ons are powered by rechargeable batteries, typically ranging from six to 24 volts. Higher voltage generally translates to more power and a longer run time, but it’s important to match the power to the terrain and age level.

Models with 12-volt batteries provide a good balance of speed and battery life for mixed-terrain use, while 24-volt versions can handle tougher trails and inclines. Be mindful that all batteries will gradually lose capacity, so check for compatible replacement options if you plan to use the ride-on for years to come.

Interactive features can make a big difference in the overall experience. Some ride-ons include Bluetooth speakers or FM radios, letting kids listen to their favorite songs while driving. Others offer realistic details such as functional doors, working headlights and taillights, and engine sound effects.

Many models are designed for children ages three and up, but age recommendations vary. Check the manufacturer’s guidance, along with the car’s weight limit and seat size, to make sure it fits your child.

They can be fun with adult supervision and age-appropriate use. Look for features such as a seatbelt, a slow-start function, speed settings, and a parent remote. Have kids ride in a safe, open area away from traffic, steep slopes, and obstacles.

Speed varies by model. Some top out around 2 or 3 mph, while more powerful options go faster. Lower speed settings can help younger or first-time drivers get comfortable.

Runtime depends on the model, battery, speed, terrain, and rider’s weight. A manufacturer’s estimate is a useful guide, but driving on grass or hills and using higher speeds can drain the battery sooner.

Some models have rugged tires and suspension for uneven ground, while others are best suited to pavement or smooth surfaces. Check the manufacturer’s recommendations before heading off-road, and avoid wet or steep terrain.

Start with your child’s age, height, and weight, then consider speed, battery life, terrain, and whether you want a parent remote. Features such as working lights, sounds, and Bluetooth can add fun, but fit and ease of use matter most.

#4518. Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

Published Nov 16, 2026 3:00 PM EST

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

“The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, said in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”

Bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

The earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into new species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

Their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now shows that it’s a snipe.

“Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as new species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

“These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” said Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”

#4516. Rimac Is Reportedly Ending Nevera Production After Selling Just 71 Cars

The electric hypercar set plenty of records, but it may have come in well under the purportedly planned production run of 190 examples.

Rimac is ending production of its all-electric Nevera hypercar at the end of 2026, Germany’s Auto Motor und Sport reports. And somewhat surprisingly, the same report suggests that just 71 of 190 planned Reveras were built over the course of its production run.

The base Nevera, and its later Nevera R variant, have held a number of records, including the title of world’s quickest car, what was once the EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and a quarter-mile run under 7.9 seconds. Those numbers may not have been enough to make the model a hit with buyers, though. According to the report, 51 of a planned 150 base-model Neveras were built, and 20 out of a planned 40 Nevera Rs reached production.

While the apparent final tally of Nevera production is striking, it is part of a larger pattern of electric hypercars failing to find an audience. The Lotus Evija once competed directly with Rimac’s Nevera, but Lotus has since moved on to a hybrid supercar with V-8 power. Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

Whether or not the Nevera itself was a success, the halo car did succeed in raising Rimac’s profile. Namesake founder Mate Rimac is now fully in charge of Bugatti, and Rimac Technology provides electric powertrain components to major cars like the Porsche 911 Turbo S. As the most significant electric hypercar to reach the market to date—well, perhaps along with the closely related Pininfarina Battista—the few Neveras in private hands represent a major leap forward for both electric performance and the Rimac brand itself.

#4515. Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting new models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company announced plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t announced any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

#4514. Bronx Zoo rescues parrots confiscated at the U.S.–Mexico border

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

“These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, said in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

The IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

#4512. The Acura Integra Type S Goes Retro in Blazing Phoenix Yellow for 2027

Acura’s flagship sports car picks up light upgrades, and a special edition that’s a nod to the original Integra Type R.

The Acura Integra Type S made waves when it first launched in 2023—Road & Track even named it a winner of our 2024 Performance Car Of The Year test—but it hasn’t changed much since then. That said, the Japanese luxury automaker is about to give the front-drive sports sedan its first major update.

To celebrate the 30th anniversary of the U.S. debut of the DC2-generation Integra Type R, which was sold here from 1997-2001, Acura is launching the Integra Type S Heritage Edition for 2027. Model-exclusive Blazing Phoenix Yellow paint serves as the highlight of the special edition, but a titanium shift knob and 19-inch, 10-spoke, Copper-finish alloy wheels are also included. Only 700 units will be produced for the U.S. market. The 2027 Integra Type S Heritage Edition will be formally revealed on Saturday, November 14, at the Super Street After Dark event in Santa Ana, California.

“The original Integra Type R became an icon because it delivered an exhilarating yetattainable, and unmistakably Acura performance experience, and the Acura Integra Type S Heritage Edition is an incredible way to honor that legacy,” said Mamadou Diallo, executive vice president of the Auto Business Center at American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “For 2027, we’re taking the Integra Type S even further with refreshed styling and more standard features, enhancing the experience of driving the most powerful, best-performing Integra ever.”

But it isn’t just the Integra Type S Heritage Edition that’ll see changes for the 2027 model year. Gloss black wheels and mirror caps will be standard on regular Integra Type S models; meanwhile, yellow Brembo brake calipers, dark gray trim, and three redesigned upholstery options are available with contrasting yellow, blue, or red perforations and accents. Other key additions include a driver memory seat, mirror reverse tilt-down, and memory brake hold. The flagship sports car will remain mechanically unchanged—not that it needed much in the way of changing in that regard.

Standard 2027 Integra Type S models will be priced at $55,995, including a $1395 destination and delivery fee. Heritage Edition Type S models will start at $58,295, and are set to arrive at dealers this December. The Acura Integra Type S will continue to be built at Honda’s Marysville, Ohio plant.

#4511. Latest Canadian budget packs funding for 55,000 new EV chargers

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 new EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of new public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, new data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

#4510. A rare U.S. coin shouldn’t exist. It could auction for $2 million.

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:45 PM EST

One of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

However, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other plans. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of new coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

#4508. Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:

This isn’t new in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

Since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”

In other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

The penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

People have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

The fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#4507. Shadow welcomes unknown female bald eagle to his nest

Published Nov 16, 2026 7:41 PM EST

Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026. From suffering the loss of a clutch of eggs to welcoming two chicks, and from losing his longtime partner to finding a new friend, he’s had a tumultuous year.

After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1). Viewers of the 24/7 livestream of Shadow’s nest could easily spot Kaydee because of her double-banded legs—a silver ring on one leg and a lavender one on the other. The pair appeared chummy as they spent more time together, sharing stick-arranging duties, singing, and exchanging beaky kisses. An unexpected twist arrived this week with the appearance of an unknown female bald eagle spotted in the nest with Shadow.

Cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow. On Monday afternoon, Shadow landed in the nest quickly followed by the unknown female. The unknown female fiddled the nest sticks while vocalizing and Shadow appeared unbothered by her presence. Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Big Bear Lake.

As this is nature, all we can do is sit back and see what unfolds. Mating season is approaching, so we have to wait and see if Shadow selects a new partner. Female eagles in Big Bear Valley typically lay their first clutch of eggs in January. Tune in to Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) livestreams to follow the southern California eagles anytime.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

#4506. Our Long-Term Ram 1500 Taught Us to Love Hurricanes

Over 40,000 miles of towing, hauling, and road tripping, our six-cylinder Ram acted more like a BMW wearing Carhartt.

Our expectations for the Ram 1500 are well established. This being the third 1500 of the current generation we’ve put through a long-term test, the only real question mark was under the hood.

For 2025, Ram pulled the Hemi V-8 from the lineup. In its place came the Hurricane: a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six making 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque in its base form. Sure, that’s more power than the Hemi produced, but some buyers hold V-8-powered full-size trucks as a fundamental truth, right next to basic arithmetic and gravity. These folks would probably dismiss the Ram’s twin-turbo six outright. Their loss.

Over 40,000 miles, our Big Horn 4x4 model was a six-passenger, 5765-pound workhorse for all manner of tasks: towing trailers, swallowing luggage, devouring interstate miles, and hauling the kind of oversize objects people buy because they have access to a pickup, a credit card, and a Costco membership.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 98837

With the Hurricane, the Ram proved smooth, strong, and surprisingly sophisticated, like a BMW wearing Carhartt. We loved its power too. Our initial testing logged 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and the quarter-mile in 13.6 seconds at 100 mph. That’s serious pace for a crew-cab pickup on Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires, and it was 1.3 seconds quicker to 60 mph than the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered 2019 Ram 1500 we ran through a 40,000-mile test. Our 2025 example repeated its 60-mph time at 40,000 miles, though its quarter-mile effort slipped a little to 13.8 seconds at 96 mph. Still, leave it in rear-drive mode, and the traction-control light will occasionally flicker during moderate freeway acceleration in the wet. That is not a complaint.

Indeed, driving the Ram 1500 leads to few complaints, which is why it’s been on our 10Best list eight times. The 1500, with its four-corner coil-spring suspension, rode with the calm authority that has long separated this truck from its rear-leaf-spring competitors, cruising and towing with the ease of a long-legged Clydesdale at a trot and making you wonder why other pickups don’t ride this well.

The Ram was a happy mile eater, as the optional 33.0-gallon fuel tank regularly showed more than 500 miles of indicated range after a fill-up. The cabin was a great place to while away the hours. Ram has been doing excellent truck interiors long enough that the surprise has worn off, but the usefulness remains. The front bench gave us seating for six and a healthy dose of nostalgia, the rear seat offered limo-like sprawl-out space, and the front armrest placed a hand naturally in line with the shifter and stereo controls.

Our most vocal complaints fell on the large mirrors from the Trailer-Tow Group package. They were fantastic when there was a trailer behind you and a nuisance when there wasn’t, blocking entire cars at roundabouts and requiring chicken-like head bobbing to see around them.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 98837

Worse, the mirrors fold and extend manually on this near-$70,000 truck (power-extending and folding mirrors are available). Also missing is passive entry, because Ram limited its availability for 2025 to Laramie and higher trims, and we didn’t notice when we ordered ours. Oops. We did go for the Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, which adds a 12.0-inch touchscreen, heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, navigation, and a larger digital display in the instrument cluster. Keyless entry should be part of that package. Having to get the key fob out to unlock the doors would be acceptable on a contractor-spec truck. Or in the year 2015.

Remote start was present but inspired its own confusion. It would not operate with the fuel tank at a quarter full or below, which seems overly cautious when a quarter tank is over eight gallons and could get you halfway to Chicago from Ann Arbor. A considerable delay from when you double-tap the button to when the engine starts raised doubts that it had worked. This is especially charming on a winter day when your spouse is standing beside the truck holding a toddler who has entered the combat phase of development.

Fuel economy was the other great qualifier. We averaged 15 mpg; our long-term 2019 Ram V-8 managed 14. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, the new Ram returned 18 mpg while the V-8 logged 17. A real-world 1-mpg improvement isn’t the efficiency promise we were told would justify ditching two cylinders. Instead, the Hurricane delivered improved acceleration, which is arguably a better bargain.

The last great frustration was our dealer’s service center and how often we visited it. Scheduled maintenance came at 10,000-mile intervals. Each appointment at Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor was more expensive than we expected. Examples included $60 for a cabin air filter that retails online for roughly half that and added services that aren’t in the owner’s manual.

High prices didn’t end at the service department either. A plastic clamp and a section of railing broke on our trifold tonneau cover, likely from one of us loading the bed with more enthusiasm than finesse. A replacement tonneau cost $2200 at the parts counter, which is curious considering it was a $550 factory option. We replaced the broken pieces instead, but even those bits cost $148. All in, our out-of-pocket maintenance costs amounted to $829.

The unscheduled visits were more troubling, because there were five of them. When the truck arrived, it couldn’t tow until we replaced the integrated trailer-control module, and that required a return visit once the part arrived. Around 18,000 miles, the forward-collision warning stopped working. At roughly 30,000, a wastegate actuator failed, throwing a check-engine light and effectively shutting off the turbochargers. Near the end, the infotainment system needed a dealer visit for an update. None of these problems stranded us or created a repair bill, but considered together, they made us wonder about reliability outside the warranty.

The Ram stayed beloved anyway, because the driving experience and utility outweighed the annoyances. Ram revived the Hemi for 2026. It’s as charming as ever and sounds amazing, and anyone claiming immunity to a V-8 pickup should have to explain themselves under oath. The smooth turbo six-cylinder is more efficient (slightly), powerful, and modern in ways you feel every time it comes onto the boost.

We entered this test wondering whether a six-cylinder Ram could make us forget the V-8. Forty thousand miles later, we remember it just fine. We just wouldn’t order one.

“The peaceful ride of a luxury car, the acceleration of a sports car, and the cornering ability of, well, a pickup.”—Tony Quiroga

“I drove five hours in a snowstorm. In 4WD Auto, the Ram 1500 handled the challenge with ease.” —Collin Morgan

“I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram.” —Caleb Miller

“I drove about 500 miles with the truck unloaded, then 500 miles pulling a side-by-side, and can say this just might be the perfect road-trip vehicle.”—Dave VanderWerp

“Nix the tow mirrors and add a proximity key, and you’ve got a practically perfect full-size truck.” —Greg Fink

“Despite creating forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas, the tow mirrors were great for seeing behind a trailer during a seven-hour trip.” —Jack Fitzgerald

“There is no better half-ton truck for a long-haul road trip.” —Eric Stafford

Our two regrets of our long-term Ram’s build are the lack of passive entry and the Dumbo towing mirrors. Ram now includes the former item on the Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, but ditching the latter means going without the helpful, but unnecessary, surround-view camera. So, scratching the mirrors but keeping everything else the same results in a 2027 price of $69,985. It might be the perfect non-luxury-spec pickup.

Thirty thousand miles in, associate news editor Caleb Miller offered perhaps the strangest compliment a pickup truck has ever received. "I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram," he wrote in the logbook.

At peace. In a pickup truck. That's either a testament to this truck's deeply soothing character or evidence that Miller should talk to someone. But he's not alone. Praise for the Ram has run throughout its logbook since the truck showed up. There's a steady stream of staffers angling for the keys each week.

So, it's a real shame that the truck can't stay out of the service department.

Managing testing editor David Beard started the Ram one morning on a road trip and climbed in to find the check-engine light glowing with the quiet menace of a "we need to talk" text. The truck seemed to be running fine, so Beard made the three-hour drive home. It was somewhere along I-75, as the Ram began downshifting on hills that had never previously required it, that he realized the Hurricane inline-six engine wasn't making full power. A scan tool confirmed his suspicion: a wastegate-actuator fault. The turbos had effectively clocked out.

The dealership unplugged the actuator, checked the wiring from the control module to the wastegate, found it all in order, and replaced the actuator. The fault cleared and hasn't returned. It's the sort of repair that is both reassuringly straightforward and philosophically loaded. Nobody who ever owned a factory Hemi V-8 has Googled "wastegate actuator." The Hemi just existed, doing its thing.

Elsewhere in the durability report, the trifold tonneau cover suffered a structural failure when both a plastic clamp and a piece of railing broke; the likely result of a load shifting in the bed or someone being less than delicate while loading it. The result: One morning on the freeway, the cover began performing a convincing impression of a sailboat. We removed it. An OEM replacement carries an MSRP of $2200 from Mopar. That's four times the $550 option price on our 2025 model's original window sticker, so we'll attempt to repair the broken clamp and rail piece first. Stay tuned.

These issues join a growing list. The Ram arrived needing its integrated trailer-control module replaced to fix an intermittent trailer-light issue that prevented us from towing. Later, a malfunctioning forward-collision system required a dealer visit to swap the long-range radar module. These aren't catastrophic on their own, and both were covered under warranty, but they add up to a truck that has required four unscheduled service visits in 30,000 miles.

What the Ram does between those visits, though, still makes the case.

Vehicle testing director Dave VanderWerp covered 500 miles unloaded and another 500 miles pulling a side-by-side. His verdict? "This may be the perfect road-trip vehicle," he wrote. "The air suspension is great for levelling out the load, and somehow it knows the trailer is 20 feet long and the blind-spot-monitoring system adjusts accordingly."

VanderWerp then noted with remarkable casualness that the truck was very stable while towing at 80 mph, and it got 10 mpg in the process. Hey, this is the U.S.A., and we have places to go.

He was less convinced by the Trailer Reverse Steering Control system, consisting of a knob on the dash that lets you steer the trailer while the truck handles the wheel. "Seems much easier and straightforward to just steer myself," he wrote, arguing that sometimes the best user interface is a steering wheel and a functioning human brain.

But for all its towing prowess and sophistication, we are baffled by the amnesia of the Tow mode button. If the truck is smart enough to detect a 20-foot trailer, it should be smart enough to remember you'd like to be in Tow mode when you restart the engine with the trailer still attached. Instead, it resets the drive mode every ignition cycle.

Fuel economy, meanwhile, has regressed. After climbing from 14 mpg at the introduction to 16 mpg at our 20,000-mile update, the average has fallen to 15 mpg. Towing—at 80 mph—will do that. The lifetime number appears to be settling around 15, which falls 4 mpg short of the EPA's 19-mpg combined rating. As a reminder, our 2019 V-8 Ram delivered 14 mpg across its entire test.

None of this has dimmed the enthusiasm. Miller is still at peace. The logbook is still full of praise (mirrors aside). And the sign-out sheet is still full of names. The Ram 1500 is the kind of truck that makes you overlook its flaws not because they're small but because everything else is that good. Whether that's a compliment or a warning depends on how you feel about those kinds of relationships.

Months in Fleet: 11 months Current Mileage: 35,410 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $543 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

Let the record show that after this 20,000-mile update we are enacting a strict ban on all complaints regarding the Ram 1500's side-view mirrors. They are massive. We get it.

Yet no matter where an entry in the Ram's logbook begins, the commentary inevitably careens toward those two opaque walls of plastic and glass that often eclipse the sun, the horizon, and occasionally, entire vehicles.

To wit, online production assistant Sarah Taylor was rattled after a four-way stop where the driver-side mirror successfully hid an entire sedan stopped to her left. "OMG, you can't see anything out the window," she said.

Other notes since our 10,000-mile update? "I'm short," wrote managing road test editor Becca Hackett. "I look like a chicken trying to move my head around to see around that new huge blind spot."

One writer described them as "forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas."

Another? "Dumbo ears." If the eyes are the windows to the soul, it seems the towing mirrors are the blast shields to reality.

Fortunately, even the skeptics concede that once you load up a trailer and escape the confines of parking lots and city streets, the Ram settles into its role as a supreme highway cruiser. Associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald gave a "shout out to the graphic on the screen that shows exactly how much angle your steering input gives while reversing a trailer." He also admitted that "the tow mirrors were mighty useful on a seven-hour drive pulling a trailer from northeast Wisconsin." Other staffers who tow more frequently have voiced similar mirror approval, if sheepishly.

It turns out judging the mirrors in a metro Detroit roundabout is like reviewing a deep-space telescope based on how well it works as a reading glass. Except you can't swap glasses because this telescope is effectively duct-taped to your face. Managing testing editor David Beard compared his experience entering a Cape Cod roundabout to a game of Russian roulette.

As we cross the halfway point of the test, small cracks begin to emerge in places other than the mirrors. We've noted a clunky 1-2 upshift and a lethargic response to downshift requests that can make city driving feel unpolished. An issue with the forward-collision system required a dealer visit to have the long-range radar module replaced (that repair was covered by the warranty). We've also caught the digital instrument cluster daydreaming: It displays a graphic of the pre-facelift Ram 1500 on multiple screens. After finishing a highway fuel-economy loop that returned 18 mpg (2 mpg better than our average thus far), road warrior Jacob Kurowicki said, "I couldn't wait to get out because of back pain."

Most other comments relating to the interior have been more kind. Technical editor Mike Sutton praised the existence of analog gauges in a world where almost everything's gone digital. Ditto for the front three-across seating, which brings back childhood memories—though we remain profoundly grateful that the nostalgia stops short of locating the fuel tank behind the seatback.

But because all roads lead back to the side mirrors, they have a throwback touch of their own: They fold manually. Shutting those barn doors means getting out and walking to both sides, which is acceptable on a base trim level, but an indignity at $68,320. Sort of how you still have to fish the key fob out of your pocket to unlock the thing.

Senior editor Greg Fink said it best: "Nix the tow mirrors, add a proximity key, and this is a near-perfect full-size truck."

Months in Fleet: 8 months Current Mileage: 23,570 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 16 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 520 milesService: $350 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

The first 10,000 miles with a new vehicle are the exciting first dates before the mundane sets in. You're still gleefully memorizing the dashboard's contours, and the factory scent hasn't yet been fully vanquished by spilled coffee (or worse). With our long-term Ram 1500, this phase concluded with an exchange at our service department that felt less like a transaction and more like a scene from Burn After Reading.

It started with an innocent request for an oil change and a cabin air filter as part of the first service dictated by the Ram's oil-life monitor. The estimate returned with two surprises. The first was the cabin air filter itself, priced at a startling $60 (the part retails for roughly half that online). The second was $17 for something called Frigi-Fresh, a disinfectant for HVAC systems.

When questioned, our service advisor shrugged. Frigi-Fresh, he explained, auto-populates on the work order with every cabin air-filter replacement. By his logic, Frigi-Fresh is not an option but an inevitability.

Road warrior Jacob Kurowicki queried: "We have to tell you we don't want something that we don’t know we're going to get?"

"Look man, I just work here," the advisor said, providing the modern-day epitaph for personal responsibility.

A memo to those patronizing Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor: Declining unwanted extras requires telepathy.

The experience is the kind of thing that makes you want to change your own oil, even if it means remembering that the High-Output variant of the Hurricane engine requires 0W-40 synthetic versus the regular's 0W-20. At least the HO's special blend costs 171 percent less per ounce than Frigi-Fresh.

While it may not have the most desirable cylinder count, Ram's Hurricane twin-turbo straight-six is compelling, even if it feels as out of place in a Ram as a string quartet in a Waffle House. Stomp the gas and the soundtrack is less Woodward Avenue and more autobahn. It pulls with the confident, linear surge of something far more sophisticated.

The six-cylinder's impressive refinement carries through to the chassis and optional air springs, which testing director Dave VanderWerp called perfect for Michigan's annual Pothole Fiesta. Consider the Ram, then, a 5765-pound limo that shrugs off road blemishes with serene detachment, making it the king of long-distance hauls. You could transport a sleeping infant in the back across a railroad crossing and the most you'd worry about is the lingering scent of Frigi-Fresh.

VanderWerp also noted that the heated cloth seats get hotter than permitted by the lawyers at other automakers, who have probably calculated the precise temperature at which a human posterior bursts into litigation.

And then there's the mirrors. We have the optional trailer tow mirrors on our truck. They stick out nearly a foot on each side, stretching 102.3 inches tip to tip. That's 8.5 feet; any wider, and you'd want a pilot car. When towing, the mirrors provide an excellent IMAX-like view of your 24-foot enclosed trailer. The other 98 percent of the time, they stick out with the unearned confidence of a cryptocurrency enthusiast, requiring geometry in fast food drive-throughs and faith-based arithmetic in roundabouts. The tow mirrors are a wonderful solution to a problem we only occasionally have.

Just a little more than 10,000 miles in, and our Ram has already proven itself as a brilliant, comfortable, and quick long-hauler. It's a machine so thoroughly modern that it makes you forget all about the guttural appeal of two extra cylinders. That is, right up until you're confronted with the 15 mpg we've observed so far, one measly mpg more than our result from the 2019 V-8 Ram we tested a handful of years back. And clearly we aren't alone, judging by the V-8's quick return to the 2026 order sheet. Sometimes, progress is just a detour on the way back to where you started.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 13,650 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $225 Normal Wear:$0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

What, another Ram? We're starting to feel like shepherds around here. This 2025 Ram 1500 Big Horn is the third Ram 1500 to undergo our 40,000-mile long-term test since 2019 (and sixth all-time), following a cushy 2019 Limited and an unhinged 2022 TRX. That's almost one every two years. So long as the Ram keeps collecting 10Best trophies (seven and counting), we'll keep inviting it back.

Speaking of sixes, the biggest change for this test is Ram's new six-cylinder engine. The flagship Hemi V-8? Gone from the Ram lineup entirely (for now). In its place sits the optional "Hurricane" twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six cylinder ($2695) that makes 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque. (The base engine remains a 305-hp 3.6-liter V-6.) We opted for a Big Horn trim with six seats because we liked that symmetry.

Between hauling race cars to track days, towing snowmobiles to Michigan's frigid Upper Peninsula, schlepping the family to weekend sports, and the endless parade of big-screen TVs from big box stores, this Ram won't be living easy. And our team's appetite for truck utility shows no signs of waning.

We opted for the 33.0-gallon fuel tank ($445), which should give us plenty of range for long hauls. We're eager to see if dropping two cylinders delivers better fuel economy than the 14 mpg we observed with the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered Ram 1500 we tested in 2019.

That truck was rated by the EPA at 19 mpg combined and so is this new Big Horn. What's the benefit of the six-cylinder then? So far, power. In our performance testing, this Big Horn reached 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and ran the quarter-mile in 13.6 at 100 mph, eclipsing that 2019 Ram by 1.3 seconds and 1.0 second.

We equipped this Ram for hauling with the Towing Technology Group ($595) and Trailer-Tow Group ($1345), which include everything from trailer-tire-pressure monitoring to side mirrors that are the size of elephant ears and boast power-adjusting convex glass. Throw in the 3.92 rear axle ($195), and we're cleared to tow 10,980 pounds and carry a 1350-pound payload.

The Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group ($2770) brings the expected modern conveniences: a 12.0-inch infotainment touchscreen, heated front seats and steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, and so on. But in a head-scratching omission that would make a Porsche product specialist proud, passive keyless entry isn't included. Yes, our $68,320 truck requires manually hitting the unlock button on the key fob like it's 1995.

Excellent ride quality has been a longstanding attribute of the Ram 1500 thanks to its coil-spring rear suspension, which we upgraded with four-corner air springs ($1995). We can now also lower the truck to ease bed access while standing outside with the fob, which almost makes up for having to fish that fob out every time. Almost.

The Ram's interior has long set the standard for pickup luxury, though it was typically leather-lined higher-end trims earning that praise. We'll see if the excellence continues in our cloth-seat Big Horn. And we can have up to six critics weigh in on every mile.
